title: H-1B Fee Hikes Could Push Talent Away and Drive U.S. Jobs Offshore, Warns Indian-American Lawmaker
excerpt: As a federal court struck down the Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B fee, Indian-American lawmakers and diaspora groups warn that escalating visa costs are threatening America's ability to attract top talent — even as DHS expands extension fees.
body:
• A Massachusetts federal court struck down the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions, ruling the executive branch lacked authority to impose it.
  • Indian-American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi called the ruling "a welcome rejection of an unlawful policy" that threatened U.S. economic competitiveness.
  • Despite the court victory, DHS has expanded a $4,000 H-1B extension fee to cover renewals with the same employer — a rule taking effect September 9 that could significantly increase costs for companies relying on foreign talent.
  • Indian nationals receive the overwhelming majority of H-1B visas each year, making them the group most directly affected by escalating fees and restrictions.

Indian-American lawmakers and diaspora advocacy groups are warning that the Trump administration's aggressive H-1B visa fee increases risk pushing highly skilled talent out of the United States and accelerating the offshoring of American jobs — even as a federal court has struck down the most extreme measure.

U.S. District Judge Leo T. Sorokin in Massachusetts ruled that the administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions was unlawful, concluding that Congress had not delegated taxing powers to the executive branch for such purposes. The court vacated the policy nationwide.

Lawmakers Sound the Alarm

Indian-American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi welcomed the ruling but warned that the broader trend of escalating visa costs threatens the country's competitive edge in innovation and talent attraction.

"Instead of imposing arbitrary barriers that push talent and investment elsewhere, we should focus on preventing abuse while ensuring America remains the best place in the world to build, innovate, and grow our economy."

— Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL)

Krishnamoorthi argued that the H-1B program "drives innovation, strengthens American leadership in critical industries, and supports job creation" — and that penalizing employers who rely on it would have the opposite of its intended effect, pushing both talent and the jobs they fill to other countries.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the multistate lawsuit challenging the $100,000 fee, called it "an attack on America's ability to attract and retain the high-skilled talent that strengthens our economy." Congressman Sanford Bishop of Georgia noted that hospitals and healthcare providers in rural and underserved communities had warned the fee would make recruitment "more difficult and expensive."

New Fees on the Horizon

But the court ruling addresses only one front in an escalating battle over H-1B costs. The Department of Homeland Security has separately finalized a rule expanding the $4,000 fee on H-1B petitions and the $4,500 levy on L-1 petitions to cover visa extensions filed by certain employers — even when workers remain with the same company.

The rule, taking effect September 9, applies to employers with at least 50 U.S. employees where more than half the workforce holds H-1B, L-1A, or L-1B status. Until now, the fee generally applied only to initial employment or change-of-employer petitions. The expansion is substantial: DHS estimates that approximately 75% of H-1B petitions from covered employers would now be subject to the fee, up from 27% under the previous interpretation.

DHS said the change corrects a longstanding misinterpretation of the law and projects additional collections of $37.9 million in fiscal 2026 and $40 million in fiscal 2027. The department rejected concerns that the expanded fees would discourage companies from retaining H-1B employees or push work offshore.

Diaspora Groups Push Back

Indian-American advocacy organizations have mobilized against the escalating costs. The Global Organization of People of Indian Origin (GOPIO) warned that the fee burden would "cripple small and medium-sized American businesses" that rely on H-1B talent to remain competitive.

The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS) welcomed the court's decision striking down the $100,000 fee, with Chief of Policy Khanderao Kand saying it "restores predictability and fairness to the employment-based immigration system" and preserves "America's competitive advantage in innovation, research, and entrepreneurship."

Industry experts warn that increased costs could accelerate offshoring. Indian IT service providers, which have been preparing for protectionist legislation, have already expanded nearshore delivery centers in Canada and Latin America. Small companies and startups — which lack the resources of large corporations to absorb higher fees — are particularly vulnerable, potentially being priced out of the H-1B system entirely.

What's at Stake

Indian nationals receive the overwhelming majority of H-1B visas issued each year, making the program particularly critical for India and the Indian-American community. The stakes extend beyond individual workers: the H-1B pipeline has produced some of America's most prominent business leaders, including the CEOs of Google, Microsoft, and IBM.

With the $100,000 fee now struck down but extension fees expanding and the broader political climate remaining hostile to immigration, the H-1B landscape continues to shift. Sanjeev Joshipura of Indiaspora cautioned that the administration may still impose procedural challenges that do not violate the law but effectively deter employers from sponsoring foreign workers.

For hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the United States — many already facing green card backlogs exceeding 20 years — the cumulative effect of rising costs and mounting restrictions threatens to make the American dream increasingly difficult to sustain.
